Retrieval-augmented generation is deployed across a range of real-world
products, not just research prototypes. In enterprise search, employees
query internal wikis, policy documents, and compliance handbooks in plain
language, and the system returns an answer with citations back to the
source document, so a result can always be checked against the original
policy rather than taken on faith.

Customer-facing chatbots are another common deployment: a support bot
grounds its answers in product manuals and frequently-asked-question
pages instead of guessing, which reduces the number of conversations that
have to be escalated to a human agent. A related but distinct use case is
customer support assist, where a human agent is not replaced but helped —
the system retrieves similar past tickets and relevant knowledge-base
articles and drafts a suggested reply, which the agent reviews and sends.

Research assistants are a fourth major application. Tools such as Elicit
and Perplexity use retrieval to synthesize findings across many academic
papers or across the live web, letting a user ask a question once and get
an answer backed by multiple retrieved sources rather than having to read
each source individually. Across all four use cases, the common thread is
the same: retrieval lets the system answer from a specific, checkable body
of text instead of from the model's memorized training data alone.
